chunks: Ibn Mahboub, from Ibn Raib, from Ammar ibn Abi al-Ahwas, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the Sa'iba (unconditionally freed slave), so he (peace be upon him) said: 'Look in the Quran, so whatever was in it, so [the ruling is] the freeing of a slave. So that, O Ammar, is the Sa'iba, for whom there is no guardianship for anyone over her except Allah. So whatever was the guardianship for Allah, it is for His Messenger, and whatever was the guardianship for the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), then his guardianship is for the Imam, and his crimes are upon the Imam, and his inheritance is for him.'
ai.seo_question: What is the legal definition and guardianship status of a Sa'iba in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (AS) elucidates the concept of *Sa'iba* by grounding it in the Quranic principle of manumission, establishing a hierarchical chain of *wilayah* (guardianship) that flows from Allah to the Prophet and ultimately to the Imam. This narration is pivotal in Shia jurisprudence for affirming the Imam’s exclusive right to inherit the rights of a patron (*mawla*) and to bear criminal liability for the *Sa'iba*, thereby distinguishing the Imam’s authority from that of the Prophet. It underscores the theological continuity of divine guardianship, where the Imam serves as the ultimate inheritor of the Prophet’s rights in the absence of a specific patron.
